title: Formats of Radio Programmes
summary: ## Factors in making a radio programme

Radio is the only medium that can reach the many poor and illiterate to inform, educate and entertain; government radio performs public service. Before making a programme we need facts about the audience: population, sex ratio, literate and illiterate people, languages, schools and colleges, health facilities and diseases, religions, power supply, nearby radio and television stations, climate, main occupation, income and poverty, roads and transport, irrigation and crops. Formats are decided on the audience's needs (language, type of broadcast, timing).

Announcements are made by announcers (radio jockeys or anchor persons on commercial channels). What is written for radio is 'scripted' spoken word. A radio format has three ingredients: spoken word (human voice), music and sound effects.

Spoken word formats: (1) Announcements: written clear messages, e.g. station or programme identification (station, frequency, time, programme). (2) Radio talk: the oldest format; an expert speaks for 10–15 minutes; today shorter talks. (3) Radio interviews: full-fledged interviews (10 to 60 minutes, personality based), short interviews in documentaries, interviews in news and current affairs, live interviews in phone-in programmes, and vox pop (Latin: voice of people; one or two questions to ordinary people on a topic). (4) Radio discussions: two or three experts and a moderator discuss a controversial public issue for 15 to 30 minutes; the moderator introduces and gives everyone time. (5) Radio documentaries or features: programmes based on real sounds, real people and facts presented creatively, radio's own creative format using voice, script, music and sound effects. (6) Radio drama (play): only human voice, music and sound effects, relying on imagination and suggestion (shehnai music and excited voices create a wedding). (7) Running commentaries: sports events (cricket) or ceremonial occasions (Republic Day parade, festivals, rath yatras); the commentator needs a good voice and communication skills. (8) Magazine programmes: broadcast at a fixed time and day (periodicity), with variety of formats, a signature tune (like a masthead), a name and presenters who link items; for a specific audience. (9) News: the most popular spoken word format; only All India Radio is allowed to broadcast news; bulletins of 5 to 30 minutes.

Music: the mainstay of radio: classical (Hindustani, Carnatic, Western; vocal and instrumental; light classical forms Thumri and Dadra; string, wind and percussion instruments), devotional, folk, film music (Hindi film songs have national appeal), light western and pop. Sound effects: evoke interest, create comic effects, create or enhance moods.

Phone-in programme: interactive programming where listener and presenter talk on air instantly; needs advance publicity; first used for request film songs, now for health programmes, rural broadcasts and complaints against administration. Radio bridge: connecting different stations throughout the country (an expert in Chennai interacting with people in a Delhi studio); first used by AIR during elections. Radio on internet: thousands of stations via computer; removes frequency or licence restrictions, relatively cheap; BBC, Voice of America and AIR are available; AIR started internet services on 1 May 1998.

vsa: List any four factors taken into account for making a radio talk show.
Audience profile (literacy, language), topic, duration, expert speakers, timing, simple scripted spoken style.
Discuss any two ingredients of the radio programme formats.
Spoken word (human voice, scripted) and music; also sound effects which evoke interest, comedy or moods.
A Latin phrase meaning 'voice of people': one or two questions are put to ordinary people to measure public opinion on a current topic.
A piece of music specific to a programme, like the masthead of a magazine, played at the beginning.
Connecting different radio stations across the country so that people at different places can interact.
sa: Briefly describe any three types of radio programmes that fall under the 'spoken word' format.
Radio talk: an expert speaks on a topic; radio interview: questions put to a person; radio discussion: experts and a moderator discuss a public issue (also news, drama and commentary).
Explain any three spoken-word radio formats with examples.
Radio talk (a 10–15 minute talk), radio discussion (a moderated panel on a social issue) and running commentary (cricket or Republic Day parade).
Discuss three information technology based radio formats, providing examples.
Phone-in programme (listeners' live queries to experts), radio bridge (connecting stations during elections) and radio on internet (AIR, BBC online).
Define radio documentaries and radio dramas with examples.
A radio documentary uses real sounds, people and facts creatively (a feature on a village); a radio drama is a play using only voice, music and sound effects (a wedding scene using shehnai).
la: Explain with examples the different formats of radio programmes.
Announcements, talk, interviews, discussions, documentaries, drama, commentaries, magazine programmes, news and music, plus IT-based formats such as phone-in, radio bridge and internet radio.
Discuss the factors to be taken into account before making a radio programme.
Audience facts such as population, literacy, language, occupation, health, climate, power supply and income decide the language, type and timing of programmes.
